column4: The warning "إِنَّهَا لَظَىٰ" reveals the blaze that calls and receives the person who turns away and hoards in 70:17-18, completing the surah's withholding-to-fire sequence.
The blaze strips the body's outer parts; this gives the hoarder's fire a bodily action analogous to the section's roasting and heat-working imagery.
The blaze calls the person who turned his back and turned away, making fire an active claimant of the same stance later excepted by true prayer.
The one summoned by the blaze gathered wealth and stored it away; hoarded provision leads directly to fire before 70:21-25 oppose him with prayerful sharing.
The people of the right ask the prisoners what brought them into Saqar; this question explicitly makes the fire the destination explained by their failures in prayer, feeding, and belief in 74:43-46.
فَوَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُكَذِّبِينَ announces woe to the deniers just before they are pushed into Hell in 52:13, completing another woe-denial-fire unit.
When the deniers are told to bow, they do not bow; this failed act of worship is the concrete cause immediately before the woe refrain in 77:49.
Those who reject God's signs are identified as the people of the left immediately before the fire closes over them, supplying the denial side of 90:20's punishment.
The accumulator imagines his wealth has made him immortal; this names the self-sufficiency behind his hoarding before the surah overturns it with the kindled fire.
God's kindled fire rises over the hearts, showing that the hoarder's apparently external conduct has an inward seat reached by the flame.
The fire is closed over the hoarders; their closed store returns as an inescapably closed fire, repeating the enclosing-fire end of 90:20.
The tree of Zaqqūm introduces the food that will boil inside the sinner before he is dragged into the blaze, turning nourishment into the opening of a punitive meal.
Zaqqūm is identified as the food of the sinner; food, the object denied to the poor in the section, becomes punishment in the coming fire scene.
The food is like molten substance boiling in bellies, transferring the actions of a pot and furnace into the condemned body.
Its boiling is compared to fiercely heated water, completing the punitive cooking image before the prisoner is seized.
خُذُوهُ orders the sinner seized and dragged into the middle of Hell, closely repeating the staged command of 69:30-31.
Boiling torment is poured over his head, joining the vessel's heated contents to bodily punishment.
The prisoner is commanded to taste, making him personally undergo the heat and severity that the section's dictionary sense describes.
He is told that this is what he used to doubt, so the cooked food and blaze answer denial just as fire answers denial elsewhere in the section.

Divorced women must be lodged where the household dwells, supported according to means, and not harmed; the root س ك ن appears within an explicit duty of shelter and material care, reversing the closed home of the section.
Those who withhold God's bounty are warned that what they withheld will be hung around their necks on Resurrection; the retained possession itself becomes punishment.
The giver is not spending to repay a favor owed to anyone, excluding social calculation from the generosity that keeps him from the blaze.
He gives only in seeking the face of his Most High Lord, supplying the inward sincerity opposite to worship performed to be seen.
The people who feed the poor, orphan, and captive explain that they fear a grim Day from their Lord; their sharing is joined to belief in the judgment denied in surah 107.
God protects those feeders from that Day's evil and grants brightness and joy, showing the counter-destination to the fire reached by those who refuse food.
Every person is said to come to Hell, establishing the shared boundary before the next ayah distinguishes those rescued from those left there.
God rescues the mindful and leaves the wrongdoers kneeling in Hell; the ayah marks the final separation within the fire scene introduced by 19:70-71.

Abraham's people answer his message by proposing that he be killed or burned, but God saves him from the fire; the repeated Abraham scene separates humanly intended furnace from divinely granted safety.

God feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear; divine provision and household safety form the direct moral background against which refusing the poor person's food becomes ingratitude.
People do not attain full righteousness until they spend from what they love; the valued store must be opened, the opposite of retaining even minor useful goods.
After the command to burn the prisoner, he is inserted into a long chain; this continues the staged handling begun by seizure and shackling in 69:30 rather than introducing a separate cause.
The dying person is identified as one of the denying and astray, establishing the stance whose hostile reception follows in 56:93-94.
His first reception is scalding water, the heated drink immediately paired with burning in Hell in 56:94.
Faces burning in the intensely hot fire are made to drink from a boiling spring, extending the heat into a punitive household act of serving drink.
They have no food except a harsh thorny plant; after the fire and boiling drink, the meal itself becomes deprivation.
That food neither nourishes nor removes hunger, reversing the sustaining food that the section says should reach the poor.
The criminal in Hell neither dies nor lives; unending suspension makes concrete the dictionary sense of having to bear an affair's heat and severity.
The punishment of Hell is neither ended by death nor lightened, another direct portrayal of fire as severity that must continually be endured.
The criminals remain in Hell's punishment, stating the persistence of the heat rather than a momentary contact with it.
The punishment is not eased and they despair within it, completing the image of being made to bear unrelieved severity.
The wretched in the Fire have audible exhaling and inhaling, giving the punitive flame and its occupants the harsh sound the section hears behind its fire-bearing name.
The condemned have a groaning sound in Hell and cannot hear there; the fire scene is explicitly acoustic rather than merely visual.
When believers ask what to spend, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and the traveler; available good is routed toward the same vulnerable people excluded in surah 107.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit; this sets a concrete boundary against the closed fist while preserving responsible household provision.
God's servants are neither extravagant nor stingy when they spend, placing generosity within a measured middle rather than the section's outright refusal.
Livestock are said to provide warmth, benefits, and food; although fire is absent, the ayah gathers the same household functions of warming and eating that the section locates at the hearth.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts people, naming the possessive preoccupation that the surah later brings before Hell.
Those distracted by accumulation are told they will surely see Hell, completing a concise movement from multiplying possessions to the fire.
After Hell is named in 38:56, the condemned are told to taste boiling and foul fluids; the burning place supplies an anti-meal instead of sustaining provision.
The flame casts sparks as large as a building, expanding the small useful hearth into an overwhelming punitive fire immediately before the woe refrain.
